front:
Confidentiality

What does it protect, and what is one control that enforces it?
back: Only authorized parties can read the information. Enforced by encryption and access control. First leg of the CIA triad.

src.title: NIST Glossary: confidentiality
src.q: Preserving authorized restrictions on information access and disclosure

front:
Integrity

What does it protect, and what is one control that enforces it?
back: Data is not altered or destroyed in an unauthorized way. Detected with hashing and digital signatures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: integrity
src.q: Guarding against improper information modification or destruction

front:
Availability

What does it protect, and what is one control that enforces it?
back: Authorized users can reach the information and systems when needed. Supported by redundancy, backups and DoS defenses.

src.title: NIST Glossary: availability
src.q: Ensuring timely and reliable access to and use of information

front:
Authentication

What question does it answer?
back: Are you who you claim to be? Verifies the identity of a user, process or device, usually before access is granted.

src.title: NIST Glossary: authentication
src.q: Verifying the identity of a user, process, or device

front:
Authorization

What question does it answer, and when does it happen relative to authentication?
back: What are you allowed to do? It grants or denies access privileges, and comes after authentication succeeds.

src.title: NIST Glossary: authorization
src.q: Access privileges granted to a user, program, or process

front:
Accounting

The third A in AAA. What does it record?
back: Who did what, and when: usage and activity records that support auditing and billing. AAA = authentication, authorization, accounting.

src.title: RFC 2903: Generic AAA Architecture
src.q: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting (AAA) architecture

front:
Non-repudiation

What does it prevent, and which technology usually provides it?
back: A signer cannot later deny having sent or approved something. Provided by digital signatures made with a private key only the signer holds.

src.title: NIST Glossary: non-repudiation
src.q: assurance of the integrity and origin of data

front:
Control category: Technical

Who carries it out? Name two examples.
back: Carried out by the system itself through hardware, software or firmware. Examples: firewalls, encryption, access control lists, antivirus.

src.title: NIST Glossary: technical controls
src.q: primarily implemented and executed by the information system

front:
Control category: Managerial

What does it focus on? Name two examples.
back: Manages risk and the security program itself. Examples: policies, risk assessments, security planning, vendor reviews.

src.title: NIST Glossary: management controls
src.q: focus on the management of risk and the management of information system security

front:
Control category: Operational

Who carries it out? Name two examples.
back: Carried out mainly by people rather than by systems. Examples: security awareness training, incident response procedures, change reviews.

src.title: NIST Glossary: operational controls
src.q: primarily are implemented and executed by people

front:
Control category: Physical

What does it protect, and what are two examples?
back: Protects tangible space and equipment: locks, fences, badge readers, guards. NIST PE-3 requires verifying authorization at entry points, controlling entry and exit, and keeping access logs.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: PE-3 Physical Access Control
src.q: Enforce physical access authorizations at

front:
Control type: Preventive

When does it act?
back: Acts before an incident to stop it from happening. Examples: firewall rules, least privilege, locked doors.

src.title: Wikipedia: Security controls
src.q: Preventive controls are intended to prevent an incident from occurring

front:
Control type: Detective

When does it act?
back: Identifies and alerts on an event while or after it happens. Examples: log monitoring, IDS, motion sensors, audits.

src.title: Wikipedia: Security controls
src.q: Detective controls are intended to identify, characterize, and log an incident

front:
Control type: Corrective

When does it act?
back: Limits damage and restores normal operation after an incident. Examples: restoring from backup, patching, quarantining a host.

src.title: Wikipedia: Security controls
src.q: corrective controls are intended to restore damage caused by the incident

front:
Control type: Compensating

When do you use one?
back: A substitute used when the recommended control cannot be applied, and it must give comparable protection. Example: extra monitoring on a legacy system that cannot be patched.

src.title: NIST Glossary: compensating security control
src.q: employed by an organization in lieu of a recommended security control

front:
Zero trust

What is the core idea, and what does it replace?
back: No implicit trust from network location. Every request is evaluated for least-privilege access, per request. It replaces the trusted-inside, untrusted-outside perimeter model.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.13
src.q: Zero trust (ZT) provides a collection of concepts and ideas designed to minimize uncertainty

front:
Zero trust: control plane vs data plane

What travels on each?
back: The zero trust components talk to each other on a separate control plane. The application data itself travels on the data plane.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.18
src.q: components use a separate control plane to communicate

front:
Zero trust: Policy Engine (PE)

What is its job?
back: Makes the final decision to grant access to a resource for a given subject, using enterprise policy and other inputs. Works with the Policy Administrator.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.18
src.q: This component is responsible for the ultimate decision to grant access to a resource

front:
Zero trust: Policy Administrator (PA)

What is its job?
back: Carries out the PE's decision by establishing or shutting down the communication path between subject and resource.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.18
src.q: This component is responsible for establishing and/or shutting down the communication path

front:
Zero trust: Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)

What is its job?
back: The gate on the data path. Enables, monitors and terminates connections between a subject and a resource.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.19
src.q: This system is responsible for enabling, monitoring, and eventually terminating connections

front:
Zero trust: implicit trust zone

What happens to it as zero trust is adopted?
back: The area where everything is trusted once past the entry point. Zero trust shrinks these zones as far as possible, making access rules granular.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.13
src.q: shrinking implicit trust zones

front:
Physical access monitoring

Name three ways to detect physical security incidents.
back: Guards, video surveillance and physical access logs reviewed for anomalies. Results feed incident response.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: PE-6 Monitoring Physical Access
src.q: Monitor physical access to the facility where the system resides

front:
Honeypot

What is it, and what is it used for?
back: A system or resource built to be attractive to attackers so their activity can be detected and studied. Variants: honeynet (a network of them), honeyfile (bait file), honeytoken (bait credential or record).

src.title: NIST Glossary: honeypot
src.q: designed to be attractive to potential crackers and intruders

front:
Deception and disruption

What three jobs do decoy components do?
back: Decoys such as honeypots and honeynets are targets built to detect, deflect and analyze malicious attacks.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: SC-26 Decoys
src.q: Include components within organizational systems specifically designed to be the target of malicious attacks

front:
Change management: approval

Who decides, and what must they consider?
back: Proposed configuration-controlled changes are reviewed and approved or disapproved, with explicit security and privacy impact considered. Decisions are documented.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: CM-3 Configuration Change Control
src.q: Review proposed configuration-controlled changes to the system and approve or disapprove such changes

front:
Change management: impact analysis

When is it done?
back: Before the change is implemented, analyze it for potential security and privacy impacts.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: CM-4 Impact Analyses
src.q: Analyze changes to the system to determine potential security and privacy impacts

front:
Baseline configuration

How can one be changed?
back: A formally reviewed and agreed set of specifications at a point in time. It can only be changed through change control procedures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: baseline configuration
src.q: formally reviewed and agreed on at a given point in time

front:
Configuration (change) control

What does it protect against?
back: Controls modifications to hardware, firmware, software and documentation so the system is not improperly modified before, during or after implementation.

src.title: NIST Glossary: configuration control
src.q: Process of controlling modifications to hardware, firmware, software, and documentation

front:
Allow list vs deny list

What is an allow list, and how does a deny list differ?
back: An allow list is a documented list of elements permitted by policy, and everything else is blocked. A deny list is the inverse: only listed items are blocked.

src.title: NIST Glossary: allowlist
src.q: A documented list of specific elements that are allowed

front:
Encryption

What does it produce?
back: The cryptographic transformation of data into ciphertext, which only holders of the right key can reverse.

src.title: NIST Glossary: encryption
src.q: The cryptographic transformation of data to produce ciphertext

front:
Key length

What is it, and why does it matter?
back: The length of a key in bits (also called key size). Longer keys make brute force harder.

src.title: NIST Glossary: key length
src.q: The length of a key in bits

front:
Symmetric encryption

How many keys, and what is the main weakness?
back: One shared key does both encrypt and decrypt, so it is fast. The weakness is getting that key to the other party safely.

src.title: NIST Glossary: symmetric key
src.q: A cryptographic key that is used to perform both the cryptographic operation and its inverse

front:
AES

What type of algorithm is it?
back: The Advanced Encryption Standard: a symmetric block cipher that works on 128-bit blocks, with 128, 192 or 256-bit keys.

src.title: NIST FIPS 197 (updated)
src.q: Each of them transforms data in blocks of 128 bits

front:
Asymmetric encryption

How many keys, and what is it commonly used for?
back: Two mathematically linked keys: what one does, the other undoes. Slower than symmetric, so used for key exchange and signatures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: asymmetric cryptography
src.q: Cryptography that uses two separate keys to exchange data

front:
Public key

What can you do with it, and who may have it?
back: The public half of a key pair. Anyone may hold it. It encrypts data for the key owner or verifies their signatures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: public key
src.q: The public part of an asymmetric key pair

front:
Private key

What can you do with it, and who may have it?
back: The secret half of a key pair. Only the owner holds it. It decrypts data or creates digital signatures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: private key
src.q: The secret part of an asymmetric key pair

front:
Key exchange

What problem does it solve?
back: Lets two parties establish keys for secure communication over an open network without having shared a secret beforehand.

src.title: NIST Glossary: key exchange
src.q: Process of exchanging public keys

front:
Transport / communication encryption

Which protocol protects data in transit on the web?
back: TLS: a protocol giving privacy and data integrity between two communicating applications, built from a Record layer and a Handshake layer.

src.title: NIST Glossary: transport layer security
src.q: A security protocol providing privacy and data integrity between two communicating applications

front:
Data at rest

How is it protected, and what should never be encrypted this way?
back: Protect it with encryption (full-disk, volume, file, database or record level). Passwords should be hashed, not stored with reversible encryption.

src.title: OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet
src.q: implementing solutions to protect data at rest

front:
Hashing

Name its key properties.
back: A one-way function producing a fixed-length output from any input. Used to check integrity. A tiny input change gives a very different hash.

src.title: NIST Glossary: hash function
src.q: A function on bit strings in which the length of the output is fixed

front:
Salting

What is a salt and what attack does it blunt?
back: A unique random value added to each password before hashing, so an attacker must crack hashes one at a time and cannot reuse precomputed tables.

src.title: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet
src.q: A salt is a unique, randomly generated string that is added to each password

front:
Key stretching

How does a work factor help?
back: Repeat the hash many times so each guess is costly for an attacker. The work factor is the iteration count. Examples: PBKDF2, bcrypt.

src.title: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet
src.q: The work factor is the number of iterations of the hashing algorithm

front:
Digital signature

What three things does it provide?
back: Origin authentication, data integrity and signer non-repudiation. Created with the signer's private key and verified with their public key.

src.title: NIST Glossary: digital signature
src.q: provides a mechanism for verifying origin authentication, data integrity, and signatory non-repudiation

front:
Public key infrastructure (PKI)

What does it do?
back: The framework that issues, maintains and revokes public key certificates so keys can be tied to identities.

src.title: NIST Glossary: public key infrastructure
src.q: A framework that is established to issue, maintain and revoke public key certificates

front:
Certificate authority (CA)

What does it do?
back: A trusted entity that issues and revokes public key certificates, vouching for who owns the key.

src.title: NIST Glossary: certificate authority
src.q: A trusted entity that issues and revokes public key certificates

front:
Root of trust: root CA and trust anchor

Why are they special?
back: The root CA's public key is the most trusted starting point of every trust path. A trust anchor is that base of the chain, pre-installed in devices and browsers.

src.title: NIST Glossary: root certificate authority
src.q: the certification authority (CA) whose public key serves as the most trusted datum

front:
Certificate signing request (CSR)

What does it contain, and who receives it?
back: Sent to a CA to apply for a certificate. Contains the requester's public key and identity details, and is signed with the matching private key.

src.title: NIST Glossary: certificate signing request
src.q: A request sent from a certificate requester to a certificate authority

front:
Self-signed certificate

Who signs it, and why is it not trusted by default?
back: Signed with the private key of its own subject, so no third-party CA vouches for it. Fine for lab use, but clients will not trust it by default.

src.title: RFC 5280 (X.509 PKI profile)
src.q: The signature on a self-signed certificate is generated with the private key associated with the certificate

front:
Wildcard certificate

What does it cover, and what is the risk?
back: Names like *.example.com cover many hosts under one certificate. If its private key leaks, every covered host is exposed.

src.title: RFC 6125: Service Identity
src.q: contains the wildcard character '*' as part or all of a label

front:
Certificate revocation list (CRL)

What is it, and what is its weakness?
back: A list of revoked certificates, signed by the CA. Clients must download and check it, so it can be large and out of date.

src.title: NIST Glossary: certificate revocation list
src.q: A list of revoked public key certificates created and digitally signed by a certification authority

front:
OCSP

How does it differ from a CRL?
back: An online protocol that asks a responder for the status of one certificate in real time, instead of downloading a whole list.

src.title: NIST Glossary: OCSP
src.q: An online protocol used to determine the status of a public key certificate

front:
Key escrow

Why would an organization keep copies of keys, and what is the risk?
back: Retaining the private component of an encryption key pair so data can be recovered if the owner loses it. The escrow store becomes a high-value target.

src.title: NIST Glossary: key escrow
src.q: The retention of the private component of the key pair associated with a subscriber

front:
Key management system

What part of a key's life does it handle?
back: Manages keys and their metadata across the lifecycle: generation, distribution, storage, backup, recovery, use, revocation and destruction.

src.title: NIST Glossary: key management system
src.q: A system for the management of cryptographic keys and their metadata

front:
Trusted Platform Module (TPM)

What is it and what does it protect?
back: A tamper-resistant chip on the motherboard that performs cryptographic operations, including key generation, and protects keys and small secrets.

src.title: NIST Glossary: trusted platform module
src.q: A tamper-resistant integrated circuit built into some computer motherboards

front:
Hardware security module (HSM)

Why use one instead of storing keys in software?
back: Dedicated hardware (or a virtual equivalent) that stores and uses keys, greatly lowering the risk of key extraction from memory.

src.title: OWASP Key Management Cheat Sheet
src.q: Hardware Security Module (HSM) or Trusted Platform Module (TPM)

front:
Steganography

What does it hide, compared with encryption?
back: Hides the very existence of a message, for example inside an image. Encryption hides the content but not the fact that a message exists.

src.title: NIST Glossary: steganography
src.q: communicating in a way that hides the existence of the communication

front:
Data masking

What does it do to a value?
back: Removes or replaces a field, for example with asterisks or a pseudonym, in a way that does not preserve the analytic value.

src.title: NIST Glossary: masking
src.q: The process of systematically removing a field or replacing it with a value

front:
Tokenization

What replaces the sensitive value, and how is it reversed?
back: Swaps sensitive data (like a card number) for a surrogate token. De-tokenization redeems the token for the original through a protected vault.

src.title: PCI SSC: Tokenization Guidelines
src.q: Tokenization is a process by which the primary account number (PAN) is replaced with a surrogate value

front:
Blockchain

What makes it tamper evident?
back: A distributed ledger of signed transactions grouped in blocks. Each block is cryptographically linked to the previous one after consensus, so edits are detectable.

src.title: NIST Glossary: blockchain
src.q: A distributed digital ledger of cryptographically-signed transactions

front:
Threat

How is it different from a vulnerability?
back: A circumstance or event that could harm operations, assets or people. A threat exploits a vulnerability, which is a weakness.

src.title: NIST Glossary: threat
src.q: Any circumstance or event with the potential to adversely impact organizational operations

front:
Vulnerability

What is it, and what can trigger it?
back: A weakness in a system, its procedures, internal controls or implementation that a threat source can exploit or trigger.

src.title: NIST Glossary: vulnerability
src.q: Weakness in an information system, system security procedures, internal controls, or implementation

front:
Threat actor

What is one?
back: An individual or group posing a threat. Actors differ in resources, expertise and motivation (money, espionage, disruption, grievance).

src.title: NIST Glossary: threat actor
src.q: An individual or a group posing a threat

front:
Advanced persistent threat (APT)

What sets it apart from a typical attacker?
back: An adversary with sophisticated expertise and significant resources, using multiple attack vectors to pursue its goals over a long period. Often a nation-state.

src.title: NIST Glossary: advanced persistent threat
src.q: An adversary with sophisticated levels of expertise and significant resources

front:
Insider threat

Can it be unintentional?
back: Yes. An insider uses authorized access, wittingly or unwittingly, to harm the organization. A careless employee counts as much as a malicious one.

src.title: NIST Glossary: insider threat
src.q: The threat that an insider will use her/his authorized access, wittingly or unwittingly

front:
Attack surface

What is it, and how do you shrink it?
back: Every point where an attacker can try to enter, affect, or extract data from a system. Shrink it by removing unused services, ports and accounts.

src.title: NIST Glossary: attack surface
src.q: The set of points on the boundary of a system, a system component, or an environment

front:
Social engineering

What does it target?
back: People, not systems. Tricks someone into revealing information (like a password) or taking an action that helps the attacker.

src.title: NIST Glossary: social engineering
src.q: An attempt to trick someone into revealing information

front:
Phishing

How does it work?
back: A fraudulent message, usually email or a web site, posing as a legitimate business to get sensitive data such as account numbers or credentials.

src.title: NIST Glossary: phishing
src.q: A technique for attempting to acquire sensitive data, such as bank account numbers, through a fraudulent solicitation

front:
Watering hole attack

Where is the malware placed?
back: The attacker infects a website that the target group visits often, then waits for someone from the group to browse there.

src.title: NIST Glossary: watering hole attack
src.q: A security exploit where the attacker infects websites that are frequently visited

front:
Supply chain attack

Where does the attacker strike?
back: At a supplier or service the target depends on, not the target itself, at any point in the system lifecycle. Examples: tampered updates, compromised vendors.

src.title: NIST Glossary: supply chain attack
src.q: An incident where an adversary exploits vulnerabilities in the product or service supply network

front:
Removable media

Why is it an attack vector?
back: USB drives, external disks and discs can carry malware onto a system or carry data out of it. Disable autorun and control use.

src.title: NIST Glossary: removable media
src.q: Portable data storage medium that can be added to or removed from a computing device or network

front:
Default credentials

Why are they dangerous?
back: Vendor passwords or keys left unchanged are publicly known, so attackers try them first. Change them at deployment.

src.title: CWE-1392: Use of Default Credentials
src.q: The product uses default credentials

front:
Malware

What makes software malware?
back: Hardware, firmware or software intentionally included or inserted in a system for a harmful purpose.

src.title: NIST Glossary: malware
src.q: Hardware, firmware, or software that is intentionally included or inserted in a system for a harmful purpose

front:
Virus

How does it spread?
back: Spreads by modifying other programs to include a copy of itself, and runs when the infected program is run. Needs a host program.

src.title: NIST Glossary: virus
src.q: Type of malicious software that propagates itself by modifying other programs

front:
Worm

How does it differ from a virus?
back: A self-contained program that propagates itself across systems or networks without needing a host program. Often eats resources.

src.title: NIST Glossary: worm
src.q: Self-contained program that can propagate itself through data processing systems or computer networks

front:
Trojan

What is the trick?
back: Appears to have a useful function but hides a malicious one, often using the legitimate authorizations of whoever runs it.

src.title: NIST Glossary: trojan horse
src.q: A computer program that appears to have a useful function, but also has a hidden

front:
Ransomware

What does it do, and what is demanded?
back: Malware that encrypts files so systems are unusable, then demands ransom for decryption. Actors often also threaten to leak stolen data.

src.title: CISA: Ransomware 101
src.q: Ransomware is an ever-evolving form of malware designed to encrypt files on a device

front:
Spyware

What does it collect, and how is it installed?
back: Secretly installed software that gathers information about people or organizations without their knowledge.

src.title: NIST Glossary: spyware
src.q: Software that is secretly or surreptitiously installed into an information system to gather information

front:
Rootkit

What is it for?
back: Tools used after gaining root access to hide the attacker's activity and keep covert access to the host.

src.title: NIST Glossary: rootkit
src.q: A set of tools used by an attacker after gaining root-level access to a host to conceal

front:
Logic bomb

When does it fire?
back: Malicious code deliberately inserted into software that triggers when specified conditions are met, such as a date or a deleted account.

src.title: NIST Glossary: logic bomb
src.q: A piece of code intentionally inserted into a software system that will set off a malicious function

front:
Botnet

How is one built, and what is it used for?
back: Many compromised computers brought under one attacker's control. Commonly used for DDoS, spam and credential attacks.

src.title: NIST Glossary: botnet
src.q: The word “botnet” is formed from the words “robot” and ”network.”

front:
Denial of service (DoS)

Which leg of CIA does it hit?
back: Availability. It prevents authorized access to resources or delays time-critical operations.

src.title: NIST Glossary: denial of service
src.q: The prevention of authorized access to resources or the delaying of time- critical operations

front:
Distributed denial of service (DDoS)

How is it different from DoS?
back: Uses numerous hosts to perform the attack, so blocking one source is not enough. Often driven by a botnet.

src.title: NIST Glossary: distributed denial of service
src.q: A denial of service technique that uses numerous hosts to perform the attack

front:
On-path (man-in-the-middle) attack

What weakness does it exploit?
back: Weak verification of who is at each end of a channel, or of the channel's integrity, so a third party can read or alter traffic. Mutual authentication and TLS defend against it.

src.title: CWE-300: Channel Accessible by Non-Endpoint
src.q: The product does not adequately verify the identity of actors at both ends of a communication channel

front:
Replay attack

What does the attacker reuse?
back: A previously captured valid message, resent to impersonate the sender. Nonces, timestamps and session tokens defend against it.

src.title: NIST Glossary: replay attack
src.q: An attack in which the Attacker is able to replay previously captured messages

front:
Brute force

What control stops it?
back: Guessing credentials repeatedly. Defend by limiting failed attempts in a short window: lockout, throttling or delays.

src.title: CWE-307: Excessive Authentication Attempts
src.q: The product does not implement sufficient measures to prevent multiple failed authentication attempts

front:
Credential stuffing

What does the attacker rely on?
back: People reusing passwords and usernames across sites. Stolen pairs from one breach are tried on other services.

src.title: OWASP Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet
src.q: Credential stuffing attacks rely on not just the re-use of passwords between multiple sites

front:
Password spraying

How does it differ from brute force on one account?
back: Tries a few common passwords against many accounts, staying under per-account lockout limits. The same defenses (MFA, rate limits) help against it.

src.title: OWASP Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet
src.q: credential stuffing and password spraying

front:
Buffer overflow

What goes wrong?
back: Code copies input into a buffer without checking it fits, overwriting adjacent memory. Can crash a program or let an attacker run code.

src.title: CWE-120: Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input
src.q: The product copies an input buffer to an output buffer without verifying

front:
Use after free

What gets reused?
back: Memory is referenced after it was freed and reallocated, so a stale pointer reads or writes data it should not. A memory-safety flaw.

src.title: CWE-416: Use After Free
src.q: The product reuses or references memory after it has been freed

front:
SQL injection

What input is the problem, and what is the fix?
back: Untrusted input alters the structure of an SQL command. Fix with parameterized queries and input validation.

src.title: CWE-89: SQL Injection
src.q: The product constructs all or part of an SQL command using externally-influenced input

front:
Cross-site scripting (XSS)

Who runs the attacker's script?
back: User input is placed into a page without neutralizing it, so the victim's browser runs attacker script. Fix with output encoding.

src.title: CWE-79: Cross-site Scripting
src.q: The product does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes user-controllable input

front:
Directory traversal

What do the special elements do?
back: Input like ../ escapes the intended directory so the attacker reads or writes other files. Validate and canonicalize paths.

src.title: CWE-22: Path Traversal
src.q: The product uses external input to construct a pathname that is intended to identify a file or directory

front:
Race condition

What is the timing window?
back: Code needs exclusive access to a shared resource, but another sequence can modify it in a timing window. Outcome depends on who wins.

src.title: CWE-362: Race Condition
src.q: The product contains a concurrent code sequence that requires temporary, exclusive access to a shared resource

front:
Time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU)

What changes between the two steps?
back: A resource is checked, then its state changes before use, invalidating the check. A special case of race condition.

src.title: CWE-367: TOCTOU Race Condition
src.q: The product checks the state of a resource before using that resource

front:
Zero-day

Why is there no patch?
back: An attack on a previously unknown vulnerability, so the vendor has had zero days to fix it. Mitigate with layered defenses and detection.

src.title: NIST Glossary: zero-day attack
src.q: An attack that exploits a previously unknown hardware, firmware, or software vulnerability

front:
Unmaintained and outdated components

Why is it a vulnerability?
back: Third-party components that nobody supports stop receiving fixes, so known flaws stay open. Track a software inventory.

src.title: CWE-1104: Unmaintained Third Party Components
src.q: The product relies on third-party components that are not actively supported or maintained

front:
Components that cannot be patched

What are the options?
back: If a flaw cannot be fixed by update, the only option may be replacing the product. Typical of legacy and embedded firmware. Use compensating controls meanwhile.

src.title: CWE-1329: Component That Cannot Be Updated
src.q: The product contains a component that cannot be updated or patched

front:
Unverified downloaded code

What must be checked before running it?
back: Origin and integrity. Unsigned updates or downloads can be swapped by an attacker. Verify signatures and hashes.

src.title: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
src.q: The product downloads source code or an executable from a remote location and executes the code

front:
Firmware

Why is it hard to fix?
back: Programs and data stored in hardware, usually read-only memory, that normally cannot be modified during execution. Updates need a special process.

src.title: NIST Glossary: firmware
src.q: Computer programs and data stored in hardware

front:
Indicator of compromise (IoC)

What is it, and what might one be?
back: A technical artifact or observable suggesting an attack is coming, underway, or has already happened. Examples: odd file hashes, bad IPs, unusual logins.

src.title: NIST Glossary: indicator of compromise
src.q: Technical artifacts or observables that suggest that an attack is imminent or is currently underway

front:
Patch management

Which steps does it cover?
back: Systematic notification, identification, deployment, installation and verification of software revisions (patches, hot fixes, service packs).

src.title: NIST Glossary: patch management
src.q: The systematic notification, identification, deployment, installation, and verification

front:
Hardening

What two things does it do?
back: Removes a means of attack by patching vulnerabilities and turning off nonessential services.

src.title: NIST Glossary: hardening
src.q: A process intended to eliminate a means of attack by patching vulnerabilities

front:
Application allow list

How is it enforced?
back: Only applications on an approved baseline list may run on a host. Everything else is blocked, including unknown malware.

src.title: NIST Glossary: application allowlisting
src.q: A list of applications and application components

front:
Least privilege

What is the rule?
back: Each user, process and system gets only the access needed for its task, so a compromise has a smaller blast radius.

src.title: NIST Glossary: least privilege
src.q: restrict the access privileges of users (or processes acting on behalf of users) to the minimum necessary

front:
Sandbox

What does it limit?
back: A restricted execution environment that stops possibly malicious software from reaching any resource it was not authorized for.

src.title: NIST Glossary: sandbox
src.q: A restricted, controlled execution environment that prevents potentially malicious software

front:
Intrusion detection system (IDS)

Does it block traffic?
back: It monitors and analyzes events for signs of intrusion and alerts. Detection only; an IPS adds blocking.

src.title: NIST Glossary: intrusion detection system
src.q: A security service that monitors and analyzes network or system events

front:
Vulnerability scanning

What does it find?
back: Identifies hosts, their attributes and the known vulnerabilities on them. Run regularly and feed results to patching.

src.title: NIST Glossary: vulnerability scanning
src.q: A technique used to identify hosts/host attributes and associated vulnerabilities

front:
Mobile device management (MDM)

What does it control?
back: Central administration of phones, tablets and laptops: enforce settings, push apps and updates, and wipe lost devices.

src.title: NIST Glossary: mobile device management
src.q: The administration of mobile devices

front:
Cloud computing

What are its defining traits?
back: On-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable resources (servers, storage, apps) that can be rapidly provisioned and released with little management effort.

src.title: NIST Glossary: cloud computing
src.q: A model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources

front:
IaaS

What does the customer get, and what do they manage?
back: Raw compute, storage and networking. The customer deploys and runs their own OS and software, so they also patch and secure them.

src.title: NIST Glossary: infrastructure as a service
src.q: to provision processing, storage, networks, and other fundamental computing resources

front:
PaaS

What does the customer deploy?
back: Their own applications onto provider-managed infrastructure and tools. The provider manages the OS and runtime; the customer manages code and data.

src.title: NIST Glossary: platform as a service
src.q: to deploy onto the cloud infrastructure consumer-created or acquired applications

front:
SaaS

What does the customer use?
back: The provider's applications, reached from a browser or thin client. The customer manages only their data, users and settings.

src.title: NIST Glossary: software as a service
src.q: applications running on a cloud infrastructure. The applications are accessible from various client devices

front:
Public cloud

Who can use it?
back: Provisioned for open use by the general public and hosted at the provider. Shared infrastructure, pay as you go.

src.title: NIST Glossary: public cloud
src.q: The cloud infrastructure is provisioned for open use by the general public

front:
Private cloud

Who can use it?
back: Provisioned for exclusive use by a single organization. Can be owned and run by the organization or a third party.

src.title: NIST Glossary: private cloud
src.q: provisioned for exclusive use by a single organization comprising multiple consumers

front:
Community cloud

Who shares it?
back: Exclusive use by a specific community of organizations with shared concerns, such as mission, security requirements or compliance.

src.title: NIST Glossary: community cloud
src.q: provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of consumers from organizations that have shared concerns

front:
Hybrid cloud

What is combined?
back: Two or more distinct clouds (private, community or public) that stay separate but are joined by technology that allows data and application portability.

src.title: NIST Glossary: hybrid cloud
src.q: a composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures

front:
Virtualization

What does it abstract?
back: Simulates the hardware or software that other software runs on, so many virtual machines can share one physical host.

src.title: NIST Glossary: virtualization
src.q: The simulation of the software and/or hardware upon which other software runs

front:
Hypervisor

What does it manage?
back: The virtualization layer that manages guest operating systems on a host and controls instruction flow between guests and hardware. Compromise of it affects every guest.

src.title: NIST Glossary: hypervisor
src.q: The virtualization component that manages the guest OSs on a host

front:
Container

What does it package?
back: An application and its dependencies packaged to run in an isolated environment, lighter than a full VM because it shares the host kernel.

src.title: NIST Glossary: container
src.q: A method for packaging and securely running an application within an application virtualization environment

front:
Snapshot

What does it capture?
back: The state of a running VM image, stored as differences from the base image. Handy for rollback, not a replacement for backups.

src.title: NIST Glossary: snapshot
src.q: A record of the state of a running image

front:
Software-defined networking (SDN)

What does it separate or program?
back: Network behavior is initialized, controlled and changed dynamically through open interfaces and software, instead of device-by-device configuration.

src.title: RFC 7426: SDN Layers and Architecture Terminology
src.q: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) refers to a new approach for network programmability

front:
Industrial control system (ICS)

What does it control?
back: Systems that control industrial processes such as manufacturing and distribution. Availability and safety matter most, and patching is often hard.

src.title: NIST Glossary: industrial control system
src.q: An information system used to control industrial processes such as manufacturing

front:
SCADA

What distances does it work over?
back: Computerized systems that gather data and apply operational controls over long distances, such as power grids and pipelines.

src.title: NIST Glossary: SCADA
src.q: A generic name for a computerized system that is capable of gathering and processing data and applying operational controls over long distances

front:
Internet of Things (IoT)

Why is it a security concern?
back: Sensors, controllers and appliances connected to the internet. Often weak default credentials and little patching, which widens the attack surface.

src.title: NIST Glossary: internet of things
src.q: user or industrial devices that are connected to the internet

front:
Air gap

What connection is allowed?
back: No physical connection, and any data transfer is manual under human control. Strongest isolation, but removable media can still bridge it.

src.title: NIST Glossary: air gap
src.q: any logical connection is not automated

front:
Demilitarized zone (DMZ)

Where does it sit and what goes in it?
back: A perimeter segment between internal and external networks that holds externally reachable services, such as web servers, so the internal network stays protected.

src.title: NIST Glossary: demilitarized zone
src.q: Perimeter network segment that is logically between internal and external networks

front:
Firewall

What does it do?
back: A gateway that limits access between networks according to security policy. Rules allow or deny traffic by address, port and state.

src.title: NIST Glossary: firewall
src.q: A gateway that limits access between networks in accordance with local security policy

front:
Proxy server

What does it do?
back: Handles clients' requests by forwarding them to other servers. Allows content filtering, caching and hiding client addresses.

src.title: NIST Glossary: proxy server
src.q: A server that services the requests of its clients by forwarding those requests to other servers

front:
Intrusion prevention system (IPS)

How does it differ from an IDS?
back: Detects intrusive activity and also tries to stop it, ideally before it reaches its target. Sits inline, so a fault can disrupt traffic.

src.title: NIST Glossary: intrusion prevention system
src.q: A system that can detect an intrusive activity and also attempt to stop the activity

front:
Bastion host

Why is it hardened?
back: A special-purpose computer exposed on a network and designed and configured to withstand attacks. Admins reach internal systems through it (jump server pattern).

src.title: NIST Glossary: bastion host
src.q: A special purpose computer on a network specifically designed and configured to withstand attacks

front:
Fail-secure vs fail-safe

What does each protect when a device fails?
back: Fail-secure keeps the secure state on failure (a door stays locked). Fail-safe prevents damage to people and property (a door unlocks). Choose by which risk matters more.

src.title: NIST Glossary: fail secure
src.q: prevents loss of secure state when a failure occurs

front:
Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)

What is it?
back: A framework for adding authentication methods to a protocol in a standard way. Used with 802.1X port-based access control on wired and wireless networks.

src.title: NIST Glossary: EAP
src.q: A framework for adding arbitrary authentication methods in a standardized way to any protocol

front:
Virtual private network (VPN)

What does it create?
back: A protected link over a shared network using tunneling and security controls, giving the impression of a dedicated line.

src.title: NIST Glossary: virtual private network
src.q: Protected information system link utilizing tunneling, security controls, and endpoint address translation

front:
IPsec

What services does it provide?
back: Cryptographic security for IPv4 and IPv6: access control, connectionless integrity, data origin authentication and replay protection. Used for VPN tunnels.

src.title: NIST Glossary: IPsec
src.q: cryptographically-based security for IPv4 and IPv6

front:
Personally identifiable information (PII)

What counts?
back: Information that can distinguish or trace a person's identity, like name, SSN or biometrics, alone or combined with other data. Regulated data.

src.title: NIST Glossary: PII
src.q: Information that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual

front:
Controlled unclassified information (CUI)

Who defines it?
back: Government-created or government-held information that a law, regulation or policy requires to be protected, though it is not classified.

src.title: NIST Glossary: CUI
src.q: Information the Government creates or possesses

front:
Proprietary information

What does it include?
back: Business information such as financial data, research and trade secrets that gives a company its edge. Protected by contracts and access controls.

src.title: NIST Glossary: proprietary information
src.q: Material and information relating to or associated with a company

front:
Sensitive information

What makes data sensitive?
back: Information whose loss, misuse or unauthorized access or modification could harm interests or individuals' privacy. Classification drives handling rules.

src.title: NIST Glossary: sensitive information
src.q: the loss, misuse, or unauthorized access to or modification of

front:
Data loss prevention (DLP)

Which data states does it cover?
back: Identifies, monitors and protects data in use (endpoint), in motion (network) and at rest (storage) with deep content inspection and policy.

src.title: NIST Glossary: data loss prevention
src.q: to identify, monitor, and protect data in use

front:
High availability

What feature delivers it?
back: A failover feature that keeps service up during device or component interruptions, usually through redundant components.

src.title: NIST Glossary: high availability
src.q: A failover feature to ensure availability during device or component interruptions

front:
Failover

Who triggers it?
back: Automatic switch to a redundant or standby system when the active one fails, typically without human intervention.

src.title: NIST Glossary: failover
src.q: The capability to switch over automatically

front:
Fault tolerance

What does the system keep doing?
back: Continuing to run properly when one or more components fail, through redundancy such as RAID, dual power supplies and clustering.

src.title: NIST Glossary: fault tolerance
src.q: The ability of a system to continue to run when one or more component(s) of the system fails

front:
Hot site

How ready is it?
back: A fully operational offsite facility with hardware and software, ready to take over almost immediately. Fastest and most expensive.

src.title: NIST Glossary: hot site
src.q: A fully operational offsite data processing facility equipped with hardware and software

front:
Warm site

How ready is it?
back: A conditioned work space partially equipped with systems and telecom to support relocated operations. Hours to days to activate.

src.title: NIST Glossary: warm site
src.q: An environmentally conditioned work space that is partially equipped

front:
Cold site

What does it lack?
back: Has power and physical space but no computer equipment in place. Cheapest, slowest to recover.

src.title: NIST Glossary: cold site
src.q: A backup facility that has the necessary electrical and physical components of a computer facility

front:
Recovery time objective (RTO)

What does it measure?
back: How long a system can be in recovery before harming the mission. Sets how fast you must restore.

src.title: NIST Glossary: recovery time objective
src.q: The overall length of time an information system

front:
Recovery point objective (RPO)

What does it measure?
back: The point in time to which data must be recovered after an outage. Sets how much data loss is acceptable, and so how often to back up.

src.title: NIST Glossary: recovery point objective
src.q: The point in time to which data must be recovered after an outage

front:
Backup

What is its purpose?
back: A copy of files and programs made so they can be recovered. Keep copies offsite, encrypt them and test restores.

src.title: NIST Glossary: backup
src.q: A copy of files and programs made to facilitate recovery if necessary

front:
Uninterruptible power supply (UPS)

How long does it run devices?
back: A battery unit that keeps connected devices running for a short time after power is lost. Bridges to a generator or clean shutdown.

src.title: NIST Glossary: UPS
src.q: A device with an internal battery that allows connected devices to run for at least a short time

front:
Tabletop exercise

How is the plan tested?
back: A discussion-based exercise where people with roles in a plan meet and talk through their responsibilities to validate it. Low cost, no systems touched.

src.title: NIST Glossary: tabletop exercise
src.q: A discussion-based exercise where personnel with roles and responsibilities in a particular IT plan meet

front:
Business continuity plan (BCP)

What does it keep going?
back: Documented instructions for sustaining mission and business processes during and after a significant disruption.

src.title: NIST Glossary: business continuity plan
src.q: The documentation of a predetermined set of instructions or procedures

front:
Continuity of operations plan (COOP)

What does it guide?
back: Management policy and procedures guiding the enterprise response to major loss of capability or damage to facilities.

src.title: NIST Glossary: continuity of operations plan
src.q: Management policy and procedures used to guide an enterprise response to a major loss of enterprise capability

front:
Disaster recovery plan (DRP)

What does it focus on?
back: Procedures to restore systems and capability after a loss. Narrower than BCP: it covers IT recovery.

src.title: NIST Glossary: disaster recovery plan
src.q: Management policy and procedures used to guide an enterprise response to a perceived loss of mission capability

front:
Audit log

What does it record?
back: A chronological record of system activities, including accesses and operations performed. Evidence for investigations and accountability.

src.title: NIST Glossary: audit log
src.q: A chronological record of system activities, including records of system accesses and operations performed

front:
Log management

What steps does it cover?
back: Generating, transmitting, storing, analyzing and disposing of log data. Protect logs from tampering and set retention.

src.title: NIST Glossary: log management
src.q: The process for generating, transmitting, storing, analyzing, and disposing of log data

front:
SIEM

What does it do with logs?
back: Centralizes logging for many log types, then correlates events and raises alerts.

src.title: NIST Glossary: SIEM
src.q: A program that provides centralized logging capabilities for a variety of log types

front:
Syslog

What does it standardize?
back: A log entry format and a transport mechanism, so devices can send event messages to a central collector.

src.title: RFC 5424: The Syslog Protocol
src.q: This document describes the syslog protocol, which is used to convey event notification messages

front:
SNMP

What is it used for?
back: A framework for managing and monitoring network devices. Devices can send traps to a manager. Use SNMPv3 for authentication and encryption.

src.title: RFC 3411: SNMP Management Frameworks
src.q: The architecture is designed to be modular to allow the evolution of the SNMP protocol standards over time

front:
Packet capture

What does a packet sniffer record?
back: Observes and records network traffic, capturing packets from wired or wireless networks. Useful for investigation and troubleshooting.

src.title: NIST Glossary: packet sniffer
src.q: Software that monitors network traffic on wired or wireless networks and captures packets

front:
False positive

What went wrong?
back: A scanner reports a vulnerability that is not actually present, or a tool flags benign content as malicious. Confirm findings before acting.

src.title: NIST Glossary: false positive
src.q: An alert that incorrectly indicates that a vulnerability is present

front:
False negative

Why is it worse than a false positive?
back: A tool meant to detect a threat fails to do so, so the problem goes unseen and unfixed.

src.title: NIST Glossary: false negative
src.q: An instance in which a security tool intended to detect a particular threat fails to do so

front:
CVE

What does an entry contain?
back: A public list of known vulnerabilities, each with an ID number, a description and at least one public reference.

src.title: NIST Glossary: CVE
src.q: containing an identification number, a description, and at least one public reference

front:
CVSS

What does it communicate?
back: A standard way to describe vulnerability characteristics and rate relative severity, used to prioritize fixes.

src.title: NIST Glossary: CVSS
src.q: An SCAP specification for communicating the characteristics of vulnerabilities and measuring their relative severity

front:
CVSS metric groups

Name the three.
back: Base (intrinsic, constant), Temporal (changes over time) and Environmental (specific to the user's environment).

src.title: FIRST: CVSS v3.1 Specification
src.q: CVSS consists of three metric groups: Base, Temporal, and Environmental

front:
Risk tolerance

How does it affect remediation?
back: The level of risk an entity is willing to assume to achieve a desired result. Low tolerance means faster fixes or stricter compensating controls.

src.title: NIST Glossary: risk tolerance
src.q: The level of risk an entity is willing to assume in order to achieve a potential desired result

front:
Bug bounty

Who is paid, and for what?
back: Rewards individuals for reporting software flaws that could be exploited. A form of responsible disclosure.

src.title: NIST Glossary: bug bounty
src.q: A method of compensating individuals for reporting software errors, flaws, or faults

front:
Threat intelligence

What makes information intelligence?
back: Threat information that is analyzed and given context so it supports decisions. Feeds help identify vulnerabilities and indicators.

src.title: NIST Glossary: threat intelligence
src.q: Threat information that has been aggregated, transformed, analyzed, interpreted, or enriched

front:
Media sanitization

What is the goal?
back: Make data on media unrecoverable by both logical and state-of-the-art laboratory techniques before reuse or disposal.

src.title: NIST Glossary: media sanitization
src.q: The actions taken to render data written on media unrecoverable

front:
Sanitization: Clear

What threat does it defend against?
back: Logical techniques (overwrite, factory reset) that protect against simple non-invasive recovery. Media can be reused.

src.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1
src.q: Clear applies logical techniques to sanitize data in all user-addressable storage locations

front:
Sanitization: Purge

What can it defeat?
back: Physical or logical techniques that make recovery infeasible even with state-of-the-art lab techniques. Examples: cryptographic erase, degaussing.

src.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1
src.q: Purge applies physical or logical techniques that render Target Data recovery infeasible

front:
Sanitization: Destroy

Can the media be reused?
back: Makes recovery infeasible and the media unusable for storage. Examples: shredding, incineration, pulverizing.

src.title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1
src.q: Destroy renders Target Data recovery infeasible using state of the art laboratory

front:
Media disposal

When can media be released?
back: After the decision that media holds no sensitive data, either because it never did or because sanitization removed it. Record the decision.

src.title: NIST Glossary: disposal
src.q: A release outcome following the decision that media does not contain sensitive data

front:
Antivirus

What does it do?
back: Monitors a computer or network to identify major types of malware and prevent or contain incidents. Signature and behavior based.

src.title: NIST Glossary: antivirus software
src.q: A program that monitors a computer or network to identify all major types of malware

front:
SPF

What does the domain owner publish?
back: A DNS record listing the hosts allowed to send mail for the domain, so receivers can check the sending server.

src.title: RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
src.q: whereby ADministrative Management Domains (ADMDs) can explicitly authorize the hosts that are allowed to use their domain names

front:
DKIM

What does it add to a message?
back: A cryptographic signature tied to the signing domain, which receivers verify with a public key in DNS. Shows origin and integrity.

src.title: RFC 6376: DKIM Signatures
src.q: permits a person, role, or organization that owns the signing domain to claim some responsibility for a message

front:
DMARC

What does it add on top of SPF and DKIM?
back: A domain-level policy for how receivers should handle failures, plus reporting back to the domain owner.

src.title: RFC 7489: DMARC
src.q: is a scalable mechanism by which a mail-originating organization can express domain-level policies

front:
Identity proofing

What is established?
back: Providing enough information (history, documents, credentials) to establish that a person is who they claim, before issuing an account.

src.title: NIST Glossary: identity proofing
src.q: The process of providing sufficient information (e.g., identity history, credentials, documents) to establish an identity

front:
Single sign-on (SSO)

What do users gain and what is the risk?
back: One account and authenticators access multiple applications seamlessly, usually through federation. One compromised login exposes many apps.

src.title: NIST Glossary: single sign-on
src.q: An authentication process by which one account and its authenticators are used to access multiple applications

front:
Federation

What crosses the boundary?
back: Identity and authentication information conveyed across a set of networked systems that trust each other.

src.title: NIST Glossary: federation
src.q: A process that allows for the conveyance of identity and authentication information across a set of networked systems

front:
SAML

What does it exchange?
back: XML-based requests and responses carrying assertions about subjects between online partners, typically for browser SSO.

src.title: NIST Glossary: SAML
src.q: A protocol consisting of XML-based request and response message formats for exchanging security information

front:
OAuth 2.0

What does it authorize?
back: Lets a third-party application obtain limited access to a service on a user's behalf. Authorization, not authentication.

src.title: RFC 6749: OAuth 2.0
src.q: The OAuth 2.0 authorization framework enables a third-party application to obtain limited access to an HTTP service

front:
LDAP

What does it provide?
back: Access to distributed directory services, the usual store of users and groups. Active Directory speaks LDAP.

src.title: RFC 4511: LDAP
src.q: LDAP provides access to distributed directory services

front:
Kerberos

What problem does it solve?
back: Lets two parties exchange private information across a public network using tickets from a trusted third party. Core of Active Directory.

src.title: NIST Glossary: Kerberos
src.q: An authentication system developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

front:
Discretionary access control (DAC)

Who sets permissions?
back: The object's owner (or anyone authorized by them) decides who gets access.

src.title: NIST Glossary: DAC
src.q: leaves a certain amount of access control to the discretion of the object

front:
Mandatory access control (MAC)

Who sets permissions?
back: A central authority sets policy by labels, and users cannot change access rights. Typical of military systems.

src.title: NIST Glossary: MAC
src.q: access control policy decisions are made by a central authority

front:
Role-based access control (RBAC)

What do permissions attach to?
back: Roles, not individuals. Users get a role and inherit its permitted actions.

src.title: NIST Glossary: RBAC
src.q: permitted actions on resources are identified with roles rather than with individual subject identities

front:
Attribute-based access control (ABAC)

What drives the decision?
back: Attributes of the subject and the object (like department, clearance, time), compared to policy at request time.

src.title: NIST Glossary: ABAC
src.q: access is mediated based on attributes associated with subjects (requesters) and the objects to be accessed

front:
Biometrics

What is measured?
back: A measurable physical or behavioral trait, like fingerprint, face or iris, used to recognize or verify identity. A "something you are" factor.

src.title: NIST Glossary: biometrics
src.q: A measurable physical characteristic or personal behavioral trait used to recognize the identity

front:
Multi-factor authentication (MFA)

How much confidence does it add?
back: Proves control of more than one kind of authenticator (know, have, are). NIST AAL2 requires it for high confidence the claimant controls the account.

src.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4
src.q: AAL2 provides high confidence that the claimant controls one or more authenticators

front:
Incident

What qualifies?
back: An occurrence that actually or potentially jeopardizes confidentiality, integrity or availability, or violates security policy.

src.title: NIST Glossary: incident
src.q: An occurrence that actually or potentially jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system

front:
Incident response life cycle

Name the phases in order.
back: Preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, then post-incident activity. It loops back to detection during handling.

src.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2
src.q: the major phases of the incident response process

front:
IR: Preparation

What is covered?
back: Building the response capability and also preventing incidents by securing systems, networks and applications.

src.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2
src.q: Incident response methodologies typically emphasize preparation

front:
IR: Containment

Why is it done early?
back: Stops the incident from overwhelming resources or increasing damage. Choose a strategy per incident.

src.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2
src.q: Containment is important before an incident overwhelms resources or increases damage

front:
IR: Eradication

What gets removed?
back: Delete malware, disable breached accounts, and mitigate the exploited vulnerabilities on all affected hosts.

src.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2
src.q: After an incident has been contained, eradication may be necessary to eliminate components of the incident

front:
IR: Recovery

What is restored?
back: Executing contingency plan activities to restore business functions and systems to normal.

src.title: NIST Glossary: recovery
src.q: Recovery is executing system contingency plan activities to restore organizational missions/business functions

front:
IR: Lessons learned

When is the meeting held?
back: After a major incident, with all involved parties, to review what happened and how well the response worked. Often skipped but very valuable.

src.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2
src.q: One of the most important parts of incident response is also the most often omitted: learning and improving

front:
Root cause analysis

What is it after?
back: The underlying causes of a set of risks or an incident, not just the symptoms, so the fix prevents recurrence.

src.title: NIST Glossary: root cause analysis
src.q: A principle-based, systems approach for the identification of underlying causes associated with a particular set of risks

front:
Digital forensics

What must be followed?
back: Examination of digital evidence with proper search authority, chain of custody and validation, so findings hold up.

src.title: NIST Glossary: digital forensics
src.q: the application of computer science and investigative procedures involving the examination of digital evidence

front:
Chain of custody

What does it document?
back: Who handled the evidence, when it was collected or transferred, and why, from collection through analysis.

src.title: NIST Glossary: chain of custody
src.q: A process that tracks the movement of evidence through its collection, safeguarding, and analysis lifecycle

front:
Evidence handling

Why does handling matter?
back: Evidence may be needed in legal proceedings, so document how it was preserved and follow law and counsel guidance so it is admissible.

src.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2
src.q: Although the primary reason for gathering evidence during an incident is to resolve the incident

front:
Security policy

What does it regulate?
back: The laws, rules and practices that regulate how an organization manages, protects and distributes sensitive information. Standards and procedures implement it.

src.title: NIST Glossary: security policy
src.q: The set of laws, rules, and practices that regulate how an organization manages, protects, and distributes sensitive information

front:
Information owner

What authority do they hold?
back: An official with statutory or operational authority over specified information and responsibility for setting controls for its generation, collection, processing, dissemination and disposal.

src.title: NIST Glossary: information owner
src.q: Official with statutory or operational authority for specified information

front:
Data steward

How do they differ from the data owner?
back: Enforces data policies day to day, assesses classification criteria and tests compliance. Custodians and managers carry out the handling.

src.title: NIST Glossary: data steward
src.q: Data stewards enforce policies, and functional data managers implement the policies

front:
Data controller

What do they decide?
back: The party that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data, alone or jointly with others.

src.title: GDPR Article 4
src.q: means the natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data

front:
Data processor

Whose behalf do they act on?
back: Processes personal data on behalf of the controller, following the controller's instructions.

src.title: GDPR Article 4
src.q: which processes personal data on behalf of the controller

front:
Risk

What two factors make it up?
back: How threatened an entity is by a possible event, typically a function of the adverse impact if it occurs and the likelihood that it occurs.

src.title: NIST Glossary: risk
src.q: A measure of the extent to which an entity is threatened by a potential circumstance or event

front:
Likelihood

What does it estimate?
back: The chance of something happening. Paired with impact to rate a risk.

src.title: NIST Glossary: likelihood
src.q: Chance of something happening

front:
Impact

What does it measure?
back: The effect on operations, assets, individuals or other organizations of a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability.

src.title: NIST Glossary: impact
src.q: The effect on organizational operations, organizational assets, individuals

front:
Risk assessment

What does it enable?
back: A systematic examination of risk using disciplined methods so decision makers can evaluate and prioritize risks and pick strategies.

src.title: NIST Glossary: risk assessment
src.q: A systematic examination of risk using disciplined processes, methods, and tools

front:
Qualitative risk analysis

What scale does it use?
back: Non-numerical categories or levels, such as low, medium and high. Fast, subjective.

src.title: NIST Glossary: qualitative assessment
src.q: Use of a set of methods, principles, or rules for assessing risk based on nonnumerical categories or levels

front:
Quantitative risk analysis

What scale does it use?
back: Numbers, such as dollar values and probabilities, whose meaning is preserved. More precise, needs good data.

src.title: NIST Glossary: quantitative assessment
src.q: Use of a set of methods, principles, or rules for assessing risks based on the use of numbers

front:
Single loss expectancy (SLE)

How is it calculated?
back: Expected monetary loss from one occurrence: asset value x exposure factor.

src.title: Wikipedia: Single-loss expectancy
src.q: is the monetary value expected from the occurrence of a risk on an asset

front:
Annualized rate of occurrence (ARO)

What does it estimate?
back: How often a threat is expected to successfully exploit a vulnerability in a year.

src.title: Wikipedia: Annualized rate of occurrence
src.q: an estimate of how often a threat would be successful in exploiting a vulnerability

front:
Annualized loss expectancy (ALE)

How is it calculated?
back: ALE = ARO x SLE. Compare it to the yearly cost of a control to decide whether the control is worth it.

src.title: Wikipedia: Annualized loss expectancy
src.q: is the product of the annual rate of occurrence (ARO) and the single loss expectancy (SLE)

front:
Risk register

What does it hold?
back: A central repository of identified risks with their details, tracked over time: owner, rating, response and status.

src.title: NIST Glossary: risk register
src.q: A repository of risk information including the data understood about risks over time

front:
Risk appetite

How is it different from tolerance?
back: The types and amount of risk, at a broad level, an organization is willing to accept in pursuit of value. Tolerance is the narrower acceptable variation.

src.title: NIST Glossary: risk appetite
src.q: The types and amount of risk, on a broad level

front:
Risk response

Name the options.
back: Accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer the risk. Transfer examples: insurance, outsourcing.

src.title: NIST Glossary: risk response
src.q: Accepting, avoiding, mitigating, sharing, or transferring risk

front:
Risk mitigation

What does it involve?
back: Prioritizing, evaluating and implementing risk-reducing controls recommended by the risk management process.

src.title: NIST Glossary: risk mitigation
src.q: Prioritizing, evaluating, and implementing the appropriate risk-reducing controls/countermeasures

front:
Risk management

What does it manage?
back: The process of managing risks to operations, assets and individuals from operating an information system. Includes assess, respond and monitor.

src.title: NIST Glossary: risk management
src.q: The process of managing risks to organizational operations

front:
Business impact analysis (BIA)

What does it find?
back: Analyzes operational functions and the effect a disruption would have on them. Drives RTO, RPO and recovery priorities.

src.title: NIST Glossary: business impact analysis
src.q: Process of analyzing operational functions and the effect that a disruption might have on them

front:
Supply chain risk management

What does it cover?
back: A systematic process for finding susceptibilities, vulnerabilities and threats throughout the supply chain, and building mitigation strategies.

src.title: NIST Glossary: SCRM
src.q: A systematic process for managing supply chain risk by identifying susceptibilities, vulnerabilities, and threats throughout the supply chain

front:
Service level agreement (SLA)

What does it define?
back: The provider's specific responsibilities and the customer's expectations, such as uptime and response times.

src.title: NIST Glossary: service level agreement
src.q: Defines the specific responsibilities of the service provider and sets the customer expectations

front:
Interconnection security agreement (ISA)

When is it needed?
back: When systems connect. States the security requirements for the connection and for the data exchanged.

src.title: NIST Glossary: interconnection security agreement
src.q: A document specifying information security requirements for system interconnections

front:
Memorandum of understanding (MOU)

Is it binding?
back: An agreement between parties expressing a common line of action. Usually less formal than a contract.

src.title: Wikipedia: Memorandum of understanding
src.q: It expresses a convergence of will between the parties, indicating an intended common line of action

front:
Master service agreement (MSA)

What does it settle in advance?
back: Most of the terms governing future transactions, so later work orders only add specifics.

src.title: Wikipedia: Master service agreement
src.q: the parties agree to most of the terms that will govern future transactions or future agreements

front:
Statement of work (SOW)

What does it contain?
back: Project-specific activities, deliverables, timelines and pricing for a vendor's work.

src.title: Wikipedia: Statement of work
src.q: It defines project-specific activities, deliverables and timelines for a vendor providing services to the client

front:
Non-disclosure agreement (NDA)

What does it protect?
back: A legal contract restricting what confidential information the parties may share with others.

src.title: Wikipedia: Non-disclosure agreement
src.q: is a legal contract or part of a contract between at least two parties

front:
Privacy

How does it relate to confidentiality?
back: Assurance that the confidentiality of, and access to, information about an entity is protected.

src.title: NIST Glossary: privacy
src.q: Assurance that the confidentiality of, and access to, certain information about an entity is protected

front:
Privacy impact assessment (PIA)

What does it check?
back: How information is handled, to ensure it meets legal, regulatory and policy privacy requirements and to find risks.

src.title: NIST Glossary: privacy impact assessment
src.q: An analysis of how information is handled to ensure handling conforms to applicable legal, regulatory, and policy requirements regarding privacy

front:
Personal data

What is the test?
back: Any information relating to an identified or identifiable person (the data subject), under GDPR.

src.title: GDPR Article 4
src.q: any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person

front:
Right to erasure

Who has it, and who must act?
back: Under GDPR a data subject can have the controller erase their personal data without undue delay when grounds apply (the right to be forgotten).

src.title: GDPR Article 17
src.q: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data

front:
Audit

What three traits define it?
back: Systematic, independent and documented, gathering evidence and judging it objectively against criteria. Can be internal or external.

src.title: NIST Glossary: audit
src.q: Systematic, independent and documented process for obtaining audit evidence

front:
Security assessment

What does it test?
back: Testing or evaluating a system's management, operational and technical controls: are they implemented correctly, operating as intended and meeting requirements.

src.title: NIST Glossary: security assessment
src.q: The testing and/or evaluation of the management, operational, and technical security controls in an information system

front:
Rules of engagement (ROE)

When is it set, and what does it give the testers?
back: Written guidelines and limits for a security test, agreed before it starts, giving the test team authority to run defined activities.

src.title: NIST Glossary: rules of engagement
src.q: Detailed guidelines and constraints regarding the execution of information security testing

front:
Red team

What is its role?
back: Authorized people who emulate an adversary's attack capabilities to improve security by showing weaknesses.

src.title: NIST Glossary: red team
src.q: A group of people authorized and organized to emulate a potential adversary

front:
Blue team

What is its role?
back: Defends the enterprise's systems against mock attackers (the red team), maintaining the security posture.

src.title: NIST Glossary: blue team
src.q: The group responsible for defending an enterprise

front:
White team

What is its role?
back: A small group with prior knowledge of red team activity. Observes and makes sure testing stays within the agreed scope.

src.title: NIST Glossary: white team
src.q: A small group of people who have prior knowledge of unannounced Red Team activities

front:
Known environment (white box) testing

What does the tester know?
back: Explicit and substantial knowledge of the internal structure and implementation details of the target.

src.title: NIST Glossary: white box testing
src.q: A test methodology that assumes explicit and substantial knowledge of the internal structure

front:
Partially known environment (gray box) testing

What does the tester know?
back: Some knowledge of the internal structure and implementation details of the target.

src.title: NIST Glossary: gray box testing
src.q: A test methodology that assumes some knowledge of the internal structure

front:
Unknown environment (black box) testing

What does the tester know?
back: Examines functionality without looking at internal structures or workings. Simulates an outside attacker.

src.title: NIST Glossary: black box testing
src.q: A method of software testing that examines the functionality of an application without peering into its internal structures

front:
Awareness program goal

What should it change?
back: Behavior. The program should encourage behavior change as part of risk management and develop a privacy and security culture.

src.title: NIST SP 800-50 Rev 1
src.q: The program should encourage behavior change as part of risk management and lead to developing a privacy and security culture in the organization

front:
Awareness activities

Beyond classroom training, name four.
back: Tabletop exercises, role-playing simulations, cyber ranges and phishing campaigns, plus topic-based and role-based training.

src.title: NIST SP 800-50 Rev 1
src.q: awareness training, practical exercises (e.g., tabletop exercises, role-playing simulations, cyber ranges, or phishing campaigns)

front:
Phishing simulation

What is it meant to promote?
back: A tactic that builds awareness of social engineering attacks. Track simulated attack responses and reporting rates as a metric.

src.title: NIST SP 800-50 Rev 1
src.q: such as a phishing exercise to promote awareness of social engineering attacks
